How to practise
Repeat mentally, at a steady pace.
Take a moment to settle in. Let each repetition have its own time.
What Anushtaanam means
A little time to know yourself
Anushtaanam is a practice you do for yourself, to know who you truly are. This app draws on Advaita: the understanding that Jivatma, the self within each of us, and Paramatma, the divine, are one.

Think of a parent playing hide and seek with a child. The parent hides, the child searches, and the search ends in a hug. In this picture, Paramatma is the parent and Jivatma is the child. The body, life and universe are part of maya, the appearance of being separate. Finding each other means recognising a oneness that was always there.

Your daily japa gives you a simple way to explore this for yourself. Sit comfortably, repeat the mantra in your mind and give it your attention. When your thoughts wander, gently return. There is time to learn.
Three ways to repeat the mantra
Aloud, softly, or in your mind
Vaikhari
Repeating aloud
Say the mantra aloud, so people nearby can hear it. This can help while you are learning the pronunciation.
Upamsu
Repeating softly
Your lips and tongue move as you repeat the mantra very softly, so only you can hear it.
Manasika
Repeating in your mind
Repeat the mantra silently in your mind, without moving your lips, tongue or throat.
For your daily japa
Our mentor recommends mental repetition for daily Gayatri japa. Follow the steady pace of the reference audio. There is no need to hurry.
A verse shared by our mentor
The Sanskrit verse and how to read it
Our mentor shared this verse to help us take care with spoken recitation.
गीती शीघ्री शिरःकम्पी यथालिखितपाठकः ।\nअनर्थज्ञोऽल्पकण्ठश्च षडेते पाठकाधमाः ॥
gītī śīghrī śiraḥkampī yathālikhitapāṭhakaḥ ।\nanarthajño\'lpakaṇṭhaśca ṣaḍete pāṭhakādhamāḥ ॥
पाणिनीयशिक्षा · Pāṇinīyaśikṣā\nSource as shared by our mentor
Six things to be mindful of
Small reminders for spoken recitation
These notes follow the meanings shared by our mentor. Your teacher can help you understand how they apply in your tradition.
Keep to the sounds you were taught
Gītī · Singing the recitation
Follow the sounds and accents taught by your teacher. The caution is about adding a tune of your own. The Vedic accents you learn are part of the recitation.
Give each word time
Śīghrī · Rushing
Keep an even pace and let each word be clear. You do not need to rush to finish your count.
Let your head rest naturally
Śiraḥkampī · Shaking the head
Try to keep your head comfortably still as you recite, without forcing yourself into a stiff posture.
Listen as you learn
Yathālikhitapāṭhakaḥ · Reading just as written
Keep the written words beside you as a learning aid, and listen to your teacher for the sounds and accents. Ask your teacher to explain this caution about relying on the text alone.
Spend time with the meaning
Anarthajñaḥ · Reciting without understanding
Ask your teacher to walk you through the meaning of the mantra. You can return to it as you learn, a little at a time.
Ask your teacher about the voice
Alpakaṇṭhaḥ · Reciting in a low tone
Our mentor shared “low tone” as the meaning here. Ask your teacher how this applies to spoken recitation. It is not a request to chant louder or to give up silent mental japa.
The verse concerns spoken recitation. For daily mental japa, you can continue silently, as our mentor recommends.
You may hear the words Uttamam, Madhyamam and Adhamam in this teaching. Our mentor uses them to describe the quality of recitation. They are not labels for you or your devotion.
Practising with Anushtanam

In Sandhya, you can count mental or soft repetitions yourself, or record your count afterwards. You do not need the microphone.\n\nUse Practice to listen and learn the pronunciation. The Japa tab listens to spoken repetitions. Listening to the reference audio does not add to your count.
